quote: Those who are better always take upon themselves the faults and sins of their inferiors. For so also the Apostle says: "you who are stronger, bear the weaknesses of the weak." If an Israelite sins, that is, a layman, he cannot himself take away his own sin, but he requires a Levite, he needs a priest; nay rather, he seeks something still more eminent than these: he has need of a high priest, that he may be able to receive remission of his sins. But if a priest or a high priest offends, he can himself purge his own sin, provided nevertheless that he does not sin against God; for concerning sins of this kind we do not easily see any remission designated in the letter of the law. Now these things we have said on account of what has been read to us. And "the Lord," it says, "spoke to Aaron, saying: you and your sons and your father's house with you shall take upon yourselves the sins of the…

But let us return to our high priest, the great high priest who has penetrated the heavens, our Lord Jesus, and let us see how he together with his sons—the Apostles, namely, and the martyrs—takes upon himself the sins of the holy. And indeed that our Lord Jesus Christ came to take away the sin of the world and by his death blotted out our sins, no one who believes in Christ is ignorant. But how his sons also take away the sins of the holy, that is, the Apostles and martyrs, we shall attempt, if we can, to prove from the divine Scriptures. Hear first Paul saying: "for gladly," he says, "will I spend and be spent for your souls"; and in another place: "for I am already being sacrificed," he says, "and the time of my departure," or "of my dissolution, "is at hand." For those, then, to whom he was writing, the Apostle says that he is spent and sacrificed. But when a victim is sacrificed,…

There follows after these things: "and you," it says, "and your sons shall take upon yourselves the sins of your priesthood. And your brethren, the tribe of Levi, the people of your father, take to yourself, and let them be joined to you and minister to you, and you and your sons with you in the sight of the tabernacle of testimony shall keep your watches and the watches of the tabernacle." It befits those especially who glory in the priestly order to observe more diligently and to attend to these things which are written, that they may know what it is that the divine law prescribes to them to be observed. "You," it says, "and your sons with you in the sight of the tabernacle of testimony, keep your watches and those of the altar and of the tabernacle." The commands indeed are certain and evident, that we ought to keep the watches of the tabernacle and of the altar and of the…

He adds after these things: "And the Lord spoke to Aaron, saying: Behold, I have given to you, for keeping, the firstfruits." Although in some Latin copies it is written "for observing," yet it is more correct to read "for keeping." But it must be inquired how, according to the law, the firstfruits are kept. For the priests do not receive the firstfruits in order to keep them, but in order to consume them. How, then, does he say: "Behold, I have given to you the firstfruits for keeping"? Whence it is clear that this cannot be applied to the law of the letter, but to the law of the spirit. For those firstfruits which we expounded above spiritually can be kept; those others cannot. But also, if Christ is, according to the Apostle, firstfruits, truly these firstfruits have been given to us for keeping. For what is so blessed as that the soul which has received Christ should ever keep him…

There follows: "of all the things that are sanctified to me by the sons of Israel." Neither is this said without a sacred meaning; for God does not will to receive firstfruits from anywhere except from the sanctified of Israel. For it might come to pass that even among the gentiles some works worthy of God should be found. For among them too some cultivated the virtues of the soul, and philosophy in some persons accomplished a little something; but he does not will these to be offered among the firstfruits. From those God wills to receive good deeds whose "mind sees God," and who have been sanctified to God through faith. But the gentile, even if he seem to have something honorable and praiseworthy in his morals, in this very thing that he does not ascribe the virtue of his soul to God but reckons it to his own boasting, such uprightness is not sanctified, and therefore it is not…

Concerning the sacrifices, several times running over these things with myself, I inquired what were "sanctified holy of holies," and it seems to me that it was as if for the distinction of those things which are holy not sanctified that here he said "sanctified holy." I think, therefore, that the Holy Spirit is so holy that he is not sanctified; for sanctification did not come to him from outside and from elsewhere, which had not been before, but he was always holy, nor did his holiness receive a beginning. And in like manner it is to be understood concerning the Father and the Son; for the substance of the Trinity alone is that which is holy not by a sanctification received from outside, but by its own nature. But every creature is called sanctified holy either by the favor of the Holy Spirit or by the reason of merits. So, then, we also read it written: "Be holy, for I also am holy,…

"And from all their gifts," he says. Someone has offered a gift to God, and again from the gift firstfruits are to be offered to the high priest. This, in the allegorical exposition, I think can hold thus. If anyone either distributes to the needy or does some good work, according to the commandment he has offered a gift to God. But he will offer the firstfruits of this gift if he not only bestows food, for example, or money, but also has the disposition of pitying and of compassion. For this is what God requires from man, that the mind itself be filled and formed with pious and merciful dispositions. "And from all their immolations," he says. There is a spiritual immolation, that of which we read: "Immolate to God a sacrifice of praise, and render your vows to the Most High." To praise God, therefore, and to offer the vows of prayer is to immolate to God. But the firstfruits of an…

The law commands that the firstfruits of all crops and of all cattle be offered to the priests, in such a way that everyone who possesses a field or a vineyard or an olive grove or even a garden, and whatever is cultivated in the ground, and likewise anyone who raises herds of any kind of livestock, should offer to God from these everything that is first — that is, should bring it to the priests. For he says that what is given to the priests is offered to God. And this is what we are taught by the law: that no one lawfully or legitimately makes use of the fruits which the earth has produced, nor of the animals which the offspring of the herds has brought forth, unless from each and every one the firstfruits are offered to God, that is, to the priests. This law, therefore, I think it necessary to observe even according to the letter, as also some others; for there are certain…

It will therefore now belong to the wise scribe, instructed concerning the kingdom of God, who knows how "to bring forth from these treasures new things and old," to know how in each and every passage of Scripture he should either utterly reject the letter that kills and seek the spirit that gives life, or altogether confirm and prove the teaching of the letter to be useful and necessary, or, while the history remains, opportunely and fittingly introduce also the mystical sense. Just as in this discourse too, which we have in hand, I think it fitting; for it is fitting and useful that firstfruits be offered also to the priests of the Gospel. For thus the Lord also ordained, that "they who announce the Gospel should live of the Gospel," and "they who serve the altar should partake of the altar." And just as this is worthy and fitting, so on the contrary it is both unfitting and unworthy,…

But now let us see how it also receives an allegorical, that is, a spiritual understanding. Let us inquire, therefore, whether anywhere in the Scriptures, besides these things of which we have spoken above, we find firstfruits named; for here he said: "all the firstfruits of oil and wine and grain, the firstfruits of all these which have been offered to God, I have given them to you." I inquire therefore now, where besides these firstfruits may be named. For if all firstfruits pertain to the high priest, then of necessity a high priest also must be sought by us, to whom ought to pertain also those firstfruits which we find set forth in other passages of Scripture. And first of all, indeed, we read it written of the Lord Christ himself that he is "the firstfruits of the dead"; he too, therefore, is in some part firstfruits. And again we find it said by the Apostle of certain persons that…

But since the discourse took its beginning from the firstfruits of the angels, which we had said were offered by them from the cultivation of the human race, and we have been led on in the following place to the Apostles and thence to each and every teacher, let us return to the origin of the things which we had begun to examine. Therefore each and every one of the angels will be present at the judgment in the consummation of the age, leading with him those over whom he presided, whom he aided, whom he instructed, for whom he ever "saw the face of the Father who is in heaven." And I think that there too there will be an inquiry, whether the angel was wanting to the cultivation of men, or whether human sluggishness by no means responded worthily to the angelic cultivation. There will therefore be in this also a judgment of God, whether by some negligence of the ministering spirits, "who…

Let us return, then, to the account of the firstfruits, which we said are offered through the angels, which are gathered from the fields of this world. But the fields of the angels are our hearts. Each of them, therefore, from the field which he cultivates, offers firstfruits to God. And if I were worthy today to bring forth some great sense, worthy of the high priest, so that from all these things which we speak and teach there should be something excellent which ought to please the high priest, it might perhaps come to pass that the angel who presides over the church would choose something from all our words and, in place of firstfruits, would offer it to the Lord from the little field of my heart. But I know that I am not worthy, nor am I conscious to myself that any such sense is found in me which the angel who cultivates us would judge worthy to offer for firstfruits or for…

Every only child is a firstborn child; but not every firstborn is an only child. A firstborn child is not only one after whom other children are also born but also one before whom no other child is born. "All that opens the womb," says the Lord to Aaron, "of all flesh that are offered to the Lord, of men and beasts, shall belong to you; only the firstborn of men shall be redeemed with a price and the firstborn of beasts that are unclean." The Word of God defined what was meant by a "firstborn." "All," it says, "that opens the womb." Otherwise, if no child is a firstborn child but only one who subsequently has brothers, the firstborn are not due the priests until others are also born, lest perchance a child be an only child and not the firstborn child, in the event that no other child shall be born subsequently.

For all this people had twelve tribes after the number of the twelve sons of Jacob. What we call tribes are as it were distinct houses and congregations of people. This people, I say, had twelve tribes, out of which twelve tribes one tribe was Judah, out of which came the kings. There was another tribe, Levi, out of which came the priests. To the priests serving the temple no land was allotted. So it was necessary that among twelve tribes all the land of promise should be shared. Having separated one tribe of higher dignity, the tribe of Levi, which was of the priests, there would have remained eleven, unless by the adoption of the two sons of Joseph the number twelve were completed.

Finally, do you wish to know what is the difference between the priests of God and the priests of Pharaoh? Pharaoh grants lands to his priests; but the Lord grants his priests no portion in the land, but says to them: "I am your portion." Observe therefore, you who read these things, all you priests of the Lord, and see what the difference of priests is, lest perchance those who have a portion in the land and are occupied with earthly cultivations and pursuits should seem to be priests not so much of the Lord as of Pharaoh. For it is he who wishes his priests to have possessions of lands and to exercise the cultivation of the field, not of the soul, to give their labor to the country and not to the law; but let us hear what Christ our Lord enjoins upon his priests. "He who does not," he says, "renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple."
